consumer_seed: The Ofcom money-saving tips page was published on 1 July 2026.
People receiving certain benefits, including Universal Credit or Pension Credit, may qualify for a cheaper social tariff.
New phone, broadband and pay-TV services are typically tied in for 12, 18 or 24 months.
Leaving during a minimum contract term usually means an exit fee or early termination charge may apply.
A provider must tell a customer when the contract is coming to an end and how much could be saved on a new deal.
Customers can check contract end timing through the provider's website or app or by asking the provider directly.
Some providers may contribute towards a customer's existing exit fees when the customer switches to them.
Ofcom advises customers who are out of contract to check whether a better deal is available.
Ofcom recommends using its mobile and broadband checker to see which services are available where a customer lives.
Ofcom recommends checking price-comparison sites when shopping for another deal.
Smaller providers can sometimes be cheaper, so Ofcom advises comparing the available market.
Customers can ask their current provider whether it will match or beat a better deal found elsewhere.
For relevant switches, the new provider should manage the switching process.
Buying multiple services in a bundle is often cheaper, but can be less flexible.
Many pay-TV or streaming services can be cancelled or paused immediately without a penalty.
A mobile customer may save money by moving to a package with a lower data allowance when actual use is lower.
A broadband-only package may save money when a customer has a landline but does not use it.
SIM-only deals are usually cheaper than contracts that include a handset.
A package with inclusive minutes may save money for customers who make many calls.
Customers struggling to pay should contact their provider promptly to ask what help and support is available.
The Ofcom telecoms price-rises guide was published on 20 January 2023.
The Ofcom telecoms price-rises guide was last updated on 29 June 2026.
Phone, broadband and pay-TV contracts can include terms allowing the main monthly price to rise during the contract.
Ofcom says in-contract price rises commonly take place once a year in March or April.
Ofcom has banned inflation-linked price rises in all new telecoms contracts.
Since January 2025, providers have been barred from offering new contracts with price rises linked to inflation or expressed as percentages.
Specified price rises in new contracts must be stated clearly in pounds and pence before sign-up.
Specified price-rise information must be displayed prominently and transparently before sign-up.
A provider must state when changes to the monthly price will take place.
Contracts signed before 17 January 2025 may still include inflation-linked or percentage-based price rises.
When a contract does not state the amount of a rise, or the provider exceeds the stated rise, the provider must give at least 30 days' notice.
After the relevant notice, the customer must have 30 days to exit the contract if desired.
A customer exercising that right may switch provider without paying an exit fee.
Customers whose contracts have ended can often obtain a better deal by taking a new contract or switching provider.
An eligible customer should be able to move to a provider's social tariff without a penalty even while in contract.
For small-business or not-for-profit services, the main monthly price must be clear in pounds and pence before sign-up, while providers have more flexibility over price-rise terms.
The Ofcom mobile-abroad guide was published on 20 July 2023.
The Ofcom mobile-abroad guide was last updated on 6 July 2026.
Roaming is using a mobile or another device abroad to make calls, send messages or use the internet.
Roaming can result in extra charges, so customers should check their package or contact their provider before travel.
Mobile companies must publish their roaming charges on their websites.
A provider should be able to explain relevant roaming charges, packages and discounts.
When a customer enters another country, the provider must send an automatic message about charges or usage limits unless the customer opted out.
A customer can set a monthly spend limit on a mobile bill.
After a spend limit is set, the mobile company must notify the customer when the limit is likely to be reached.
A provider can charge above a set spend limit only when the customer agrees.
Providers may offer daily or weekly roaming charges or bundles of calls, texts or data.
Turning off data roaming can help limit mobile-data use abroad.
Using local Wi-Fi instead of mobile internet can reduce roaming data use.
Downloading playlists, podcasts or programmes before travel can help avoid data charges.
Travellers should check whether children's devices could incur roaming charges.
Without Wi-Fi, Ofcom advises avoiding data-heavy activities such as video, photo uploads, music downloads and large attachments.
A traveller may consider a local SIM card or an eSIM for the destination country.
Accidental roaming can occur near borders when a phone connects to a stronger signal from the neighbouring country.
Providers must give customers information on preventing accidental roaming and help reduce or limit roaming costs while in the UK.
At sea, a mobile may connect to a ship satellite, where charges can be higher than ordinary roaming.
Manually selecting a preferred network at sea may avoid satellite connections, but can prevent calls and texts when that network is out of range.
Global 2G and 3G switch-offs can affect roaming because national timetables differ.
In affected countries, an older phone may be unable to make calls or use data unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Ofcom advises speaking to the provider before leaving the UK.
The Ofcom switching overview was published on 13 August 2021.
The Ofcom switching overview was last updated on 1 July 2026.
Mobile customers can switch provider using a free text through Text to Switch.
For broadband and landline, the new provider can arrange the switch using One Touch Switch.
